title: Germany's Gen Z protests
dek: A new youth initiative, Gen Z regelt, brought tens of thousands of young people onto the streets of more than 30 German cities over education, living costs, climate and conscription. Most marches were peaceful; night-time violence in several cities, and who caused it, is now the political fight.
summary: Gen Z regelt, roughly "Gen Z sorts it out", is a newly founded youth initiative that planned its first nationwide protest for more than three weeks, citing the French high-school movement as a parallel, Anadolu reports. Its demands include more money for education, health care, addiction treatment and psychotherapy, affordable living costs, stronger climate action, limits on surveillance and no compulsory military service. More than 150,000 people registered to take part in over 30 cities.

On Saturday, October 31, the daytime marches were largely peaceful. Police counted about 5,000 people at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate and up to 8,000 in Frankfurt; organisers put nationwide turnout at 100,000 to 120,000, below their projections. After nightfall violence broke out in Frankfurt, Cologne, Hamburg and Berlin: in Frankfurt, shops were damaged and looted and Hesse's interior minister said 54 people were arrested and more than 100 officers injured.

Who caused the violence is disputed. Hesse's interior minister Roman Poseck blamed left-wing extremists and people of a "migrant background", and federal interior minister Alexander Dobrindt blamed violent left-wing groups and "troublemakers from the migrant community". Police in Frankfurt said the vast majority demonstrated peacefully, and a fact check by The Local found most Frankfurt arrestees lived in Hesse or nearby states. Education Minister Karin Prien called the young people's concerns "legitimate". The organisers plan further protests in November.

Protest day in more than 30 cities
The fight over who caused the violence, and what comes next

events.label: reported
events.text: More than 154,000 people have registered for Saturday's protests by the youth initiative Gen Z regelt in Berlin and some 30 other cities, according to the group's website, Anadolu reports; co-organiser Akram Selo, 18, says planning began more than three weeks earlier, when the French protests "were still peaceful".

events.label: alleged
events.text: CDU/CSU politicians warn the movement has been co-opted by far-left extremists and criminal elements, and Stuttgart's CDU council group considers a ban on public gatherings, Anadolu reports; Berlin police say there is "no reliable evidence" of targeted extremist control over the group, Euronews reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Young people march in more than 30 German cities for education funding, affordable living, climate action and against compulsory military service; police count about 5,000 at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate, where the rally passes almost without incident, Euronews and The Local report.

events.label: disputed
events.text: Organisers put nationwide turnout at 100,000 to 120,000, below the more than 150,000 expected; police counted up to 8,000 in Frankfurt and about 2,000 in Nuremberg, The Local and Bloomberg report.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: After nightfall, violence breaks out in Frankfurt, Cologne, Hamburg and Berlin; in Frankfurt shops are looted, police use water cannon and protesters throw Molotov cocktails, Bloomberg reports. Hesse's interior minister Roman Poseck says 54 people were arrested and more than 100 officers injured in Frankfurt, The Local reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Berlin, police make almost 60 arrests away from the main rally, for property damage, assault and weapons offences, Bloomberg reports; Berlin's unrest was linked to a separate demonstration, "Gen Z hat genug!", from which Gen Z regelt had distanced itself, The Local reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: The youth initiative “Gen Z steht auf” called for demonstrations in 21 German cities on Oct. 31, including Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne and Dortmund, according to Telegraph India. The outlet also reported that no protests were observed in Berlin.

events.label: alleged
events.text: A Calcuttan living in Berlin told his parents there were no protests in the city on Oct. 31, while a Calcuttan residing in Düsseldorf said she heard reports of an emergency declaration and stayed indoors.

events.label: disputed
events.text: Federal interior minister Alexander Dobrindt blames "violent left-wing groups" and "troublemakers from the migrant community", and Hesse's Poseck says the troublemakers were predominantly of migrant background; Frankfurt police say the vast majority demonstrated peacefully, and a fact check finds most Frankfurt arrestees lived in Hesse or nearby states, The Local reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien calls the concerns of the young people who marched in more than 30 cities on October 31 "legitimate and extremely relevant" and promises more dialogue, and SPD politicians call for a national education summit; these are proposals, not policy changes so far, The Local reports.

events.label: pending
events.text: Gen Z regelt plans another countrywide protest on November 14, according to Bloomberg, and to join an international youth strike on November 20, according to The Local and Anadolu. Still being checked.

claims.title: Who caused the violence on October 31?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: Hesse's interior minister Roman Poseck says left-wing extremists infiltrated the protests and that troublemakers were predominantly of migrant background; federal interior minister Alexander Dobrindt blames violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community.
claims.b: Frankfurt police say the vast majority demonstrated peacefully; The Local's fact check found most Frankfurt arrestees were residents of Hesse or nearby states, with no police evidence of offenders travelling from abroad; Defence Minister Boris Pistorius questioned who counts as "migrant groups".
claims.status: Investigations are under way; no court has ruled.

claims.title: How many took part?
claims.label: disputed
claims.b: Police give city counts, such as about 5,000 in Berlin and up to 8,000 in Frankfurt; Bloomberg reports crowds fell short of the more than 150,000 expected.
claims.status: No official nationwide count has been published.

accountability.action: 54 arrests in Frankfurt, according to Hesse's interior minister; more than 30, according to an earlier Bloomberg count
